title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 10
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each, with an explanation for every answer choice and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, and an explanation for every question.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. والنسبة اللي هتظهر في الآخر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 10
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest items, and Module 2 adapts to your Module 1 performance (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it.

questions.p: The engineers' design for the new footbridge was widely praised for its ______: using a single curved steel beam and a few thin cables, it crosses the river with far less material than conventional bridges of the same length.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The colon explains the praise: the bridge uses far less material, so it is praised for its efficient use of resources, its "economy." "Ornamentation" fails because the design is admired for being simple, not decorative.
ce: Correct: crossing the river with "far less material" is an efficient, economical use of resources.
A bridge praised for using few parts is not praised for decoration.
No one praises a bridge for being easy to break, and nothing suggests it is weak.
Nothing in the text describes how tall the bridge is.

questions.p: Scientists have long wondered how female sea turtles find their way back to the beaches where they hatched, sometimes after decades at sea. Evidence now suggests that hatchlings ______ the unique magnetic "signature" of their home beach and use it years later to navigate back.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: To use the signature years later, the turtles must remember it from when they hatched: "memorize." "Create" fails because the signature is a feature of the beach, not something the turtles make.
ce: Hatchlings cannot disturb Earth's magnetic field, and doing so would not help them return.
Correct: using the beach's signature "years later" requires the hatchlings to store it in memory.
The magnetic signature belongs to the beach; the turtles do not create it.
Contradicted: they "use it years later to navigate back."

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The house stood at the end of a lane so ______ that the postman, a man not easily discouraged, brought its letters only once a week, and then with a look of injured patience.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: Even a postman "not easily discouraged" comes only weekly and unwillingly, so the lane must be hard to reach: "remote." "Ordinary" cannot explain such unusual treatment.
ce: A cheerful lane would not discourage the postman or give him a look of "injured patience."
Correct: a lane so far out that even a determined postman visits only weekly is remote.
Nothing suggests many people; the problem is the distance and effort.
An ordinary lane would not limit deliveries to once a week.

questions.p: Sociologist Yara Habib argues that neighbourhood festivals, far from being ______ entertainment, play a serious role in building trust between residents who otherwise rarely meet.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "Far from being X, they play a serious role" means X must be the opposite of serious: "trivial." "Essential" reverses the contrast.
ce: Correct: "far from being … entertainment" is set against "a serious role," so the blank must mean unimportant.
Opposite: the sentence says festivals are more than the blank, and "essential" would already mean serious and important.
Cost is not contrasted with seriousness anywhere in the text.
The age of festivals has nothing to do with the contrast the sentence makes.

questions.p: Long before full-colour film was common, many films of the silent era were tinted: each scene was dyed a single colour, such as blue for night, amber for lamplight, or red for fire. Tinting did not show the true colours of objects, but it gave audiences a quick signal about the time of day or the mood of a scene. After films with recorded sound arrived in the late 1920s, the practice largely disappeared.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To explain the chemistry of the dyes used to tint film
To argue that tinted films were more beautiful than modern colour films
To describe an early film technique and explain what it communicated to audiences
To compare the audiences of silent films with those of sound films
questions.e: The text describes tinting and explains its purpose for viewers, then notes when it ended. The "more beautiful" choice adds an opinion the text never gives.
ce: No chemistry is described.
The text makes no judgment about beauty and does not compare tinting with modern colour.
Correct: the text explains what tinting was, what it told viewers (time of day, mood), and when it faded.
Audiences are mentioned only as viewers of tinted scenes; no comparison is made.

questions.p: Sand dunes move. Wind blowing across a dune lifts sand grains from its gentle windward slope and drops them over the crest, where they slide down the steeper slope on the far side. __Grain by grain, the whole dune creeps forward, sometimes by tens of meters in a single year.__ In some desert towns, moving dunes have buried roads and even houses.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It gives an example of a town that has been buried by a dune.
It introduces a contrast with the process described in the previous sentence.
It describes the overall result of the process explained in the previous sentence.
It questions the claim made in the first sentence of the text.
questions.e: The previous sentence explains how single grains move; the underlined sentence shows the combined effect: the whole dune advances. The "contrast" choice is wrong because the sentence continues the same idea.
ce: The towns appear only in the next sentence.
There is no contrast; the sentence follows from the process.
Correct: grains moving over the crest add up to the whole dune moving forward.
It supports the claim that dunes move; it does not question it.

questions.p:
Text 1
Some education writers claim that students learn more when they take notes on laptops in class. Because typing is faster than writing by hand, they argue, students can record more of what the teacher says and so have more material to study later.

Text 2
Psychologist Kareem Aziz compared students who typed their notes with students who wrote them by hand. The typists recorded many more words, but they often copied the lecture almost word for word. The students writing by hand could not keep up, so they had to summarize ideas in their own words. On a test of understanding a week later, the handwriting group scored higher.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Aziz (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
c: He would claim that typists record fewer words than students who write by hand.
He would agree that typing notes leads to better test results.
He would argue that students should not take notes at all.
He would argue that recording more words does not necessarily lead to better learning.
questions.e: Text 1 assumes more notes means more learning; Aziz found the opposite on understanding, because handwriting forces students to summarize. The "no notes at all" choice goes far beyond his findings.
ce: Contradicted: the typists "recorded many more words."
Reversed: the handwriting group scored higher.
Too extreme: his study compared two ways of taking notes and did not test taking none.
Correct: the typists recorded more but understood less, which goes against the writers' reasoning.

questions.p: In many older cities, raised railway lines that once carried goods to factories have fallen out of use. Rather than tearing down the tracks, several cities have turned them into long, narrow parks planted with trees and grasses. The parks give residents places to walk away from traffic. Studies have also found that property values near some of these parks have risen sharply, a change that has helped some local businesses but has also pushed up rents for long-time residents.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Railway parks have lowered rents for long-time residents.
Raised railway lines once carried goods to factories in many older cities.
Turning old raised railway lines into parks has given residents new places to walk but has had mixed effects on the surrounding neighbourhoods.
Cities should tear down unused railway lines rather than turn them into parks.
questions.e: The text describes railway parks, their benefit to residents, and their mixed effect on property values and rents. The "lowered rents" choice reverses what the studies found.
ce: Reversed: the parks have pushed rents up.
Too narrow: background detail from the first sentence.
Correct: it covers the benefit (places to walk) and the mixed economic result (help for businesses, higher rents).
The text gives no such recommendation; it describes cities choosing not to tear them down.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Captain Rowe had sailed the eastern seas for twenty years and could name every star by which a ship might steer, yet on land he was hopeless at finding his way. His wife declared that he could lose himself between the front door and the garden gate, and the neighbours, who had more than once led him home, did not think she exaggerated.
questions.q: According to the text, what is surprising about Captain Rowe?
c: He has forgotten the names of the stars since leaving the sea.
Although he can navigate expertly at sea, he easily gets lost on land.
His wife often exaggerates his faults to the neighbours.
He prefers walking in his garden to sailing.
questions.e: The surprise lies in the contrast introduced by "yet": a master navigator at sea who gets lost near his own house. The "exaggerates" choice contradicts the neighbours' view.
ce: The text says he "could name every star," not that he has forgotten them.
Correct: the text contrasts his skill with the stars at sea and his helplessness on land.
The neighbours "did not think she exaggerated."
No preference is mentioned.

questions.p: Ethnomusicologist Samir Adly has recorded the traditional work songs of fishing communities along one coast. He hypothesizes that the rhythms of many of these songs developed to match the physical tasks the fishers performed while singing them.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Adly's hypothesis?
c: Many of the songs mention the sea, the weather, or the fish the communities catch.
Songs sung while rowing have a steady beat at about the same speed as a rowing stroke, while songs sung while mending nets, a task with no regular rhythm, have no steady beat.
The songs are sung in several different languages along the coast.
Younger fishers know fewer of the songs than older fishers do.
questions.e: Adly links rhythm to task, so the best support shows rhythms changing with the task: steady for rowing, free for mending nets. The lyrics choice is tempting but tests words, not rhythm.
ce: This is about the songs' words, not their rhythms.
Correct: the rhythm of each song matches the rhythm of its task, which is what Adly predicts.
Language says nothing about whether rhythms match tasks.
This is about who knows the songs, not how their rhythms developed.

questions.p: Large swarms of jellyfish have appeared much more often along one stretch of coast since 2010. Oceanographer Amira Saleh argues that rising sea temperatures caused this increase, since warmer water helps young jellyfish grow faster.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Saleh's argument?
c: Sea temperatures along that coast have not changed since 2010, but fishing of the small fish that compete with jellyfish for food has tripled.
Jellyfish swarms have blocked the cooling pipes of a power plant on the coast.
Some species of jellyfish can live for more than a year.
Warmer water helps the young of several jellyfish species grow faster in laboratory tanks.
questions.e: Saleh blames rising temperatures, so finding that temperatures did not rise directly undercuts her, and overfishing offers another explanation. The laboratory finding is the reversal trap: it supports her instead.
ce: Correct: if the water has not warmed, warming cannot explain the increase, and another cause is suggested.
An effect of the swarms, not evidence about their cause.
Lifespan does not test whether warmer water caused the swarms.
This would support Saleh's reasoning rather than weaken it.

questions.p:
Rainfall and landslides in one mountain district, 2023
Month | Rainfall (millimeters) | Landslides recorded
June | 40 | 1
July | 210 | 9
August | 260 | 14
September | 120 | 4

Geologists in one mountain district have observed that landslides there become more frequent as rainfall increases.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the geologists' observation?
c: Landslides were most frequent in July, the wettest month in the table.
The district recorded 9 landslides in July.
The district received 120 millimeters of rain in September.
In August, the wettest month in the table (260 millimeters), the district recorded 14 landslides, while in June, the driest (40 millimeters), it recorded only 1.
questions.e: The observation links two variables, so the answer must show both: the wettest month had the most landslides and the driest the fewest. The July choice misreads the table.
ce: False: August was wetter (260 vs 210) and had more landslides (14 vs 9).
True, but one month alone shows no link with rainfall.
True, but it gives no landslide figure, so it cannot show a link.
Correct: it pairs the most rain with the most landslides and the least rain with the fewest.

questions.p:
Average length of feature films released in one country, by genre (minutes)
Genre | 2010 | 2020
Drama | 118 | 126
Comedy | 101 | 99
Action | 115 | 129
Animation | 92 | 95

A film critic studying films released in one country noted that action films grew longer between 2010 and 2020 by more minutes than films of any other genre in the table: ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: the average action film went from 115 minutes in 2010 to 129 minutes in 2020, an increase of 14 minutes, compared with 8 minutes for dramas and 3 for animated films.
in 2020, action films were longer on average than films of any other genre in the table.
the average drama went from 118 minutes in 2010 to 126 minutes in 2020.
the average comedy went from 101 minutes in 2010 to 99 minutes in 2020.
questions.e: The claim is about how much longer films became, so the answer must compare increases: action +14, drama +8, animation +3. The "longest in 2020" choice is true but measures length, not growth.
ce: Correct: it gives action's increase (14) and shows it is larger than the other genres' increases.
True (129 minutes), but the claim is about the size of the increase, not about which genre was longest.
True, but it describes dramas, not action films.
True, but comedies are not the subject of the claim.

questions.p: Snow that falls on the Antarctic ice sheet is slowly buried by the snow of later years and pressed into ice, so the deeper a layer of ice lies, the older it is. As the snow turns to ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air, preserving samples of the atmosphere from the time the layer formed. A scientist who wants to know how much carbon dioxide the air contained during a period long before any human records were kept should therefore ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: measure how much snow fell on the ice sheet in the most recent year.
analyze air bubbles from the newest layers near the surface of the ice.
analyze air bubbles from layers deep in the ice that formed during that period.
melt a sample of ice and measure its temperature.
questions.e: Two clues combine: deeper ice is older, and bubbles preserve air from when the ice formed. So ancient air is found in deep layers. The surface-layer choice reverses the age clue.
ce: This year's snowfall tells nothing about the ancient atmosphere.
Reversed: the surface layers are the youngest, so they hold recent air.
Correct: deep layers are old, and their bubbles hold air from the time they formed.
The text links the air bubbles, not the ice's temperature, to the past atmosphere.

questions.p: The nay, an end-blown flute made from a hollow reed, is one of the oldest instruments still played in ______ flutes much like it appear in paintings on the walls of ancient Egyptian tombs.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "The nay… is one of the oldest instruments still played in Egypt" and "flutes much like it appear…" are both complete, so a semicolon is needed. A comma would create a comma splice.
ce: Run-on: the two sentences are fused with no punctuation.
Comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Correct: both parts are complete sentences, and a semicolon joins two complete sentences.
"Which flutes much like it appear…" is not a correct clause, so the sentence becomes ungrammatical.

questions.p: The city's new library includes a rooftop garden, a recording studio for local ______ and a hall that can seat four hundred people.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: This is a simple list of three items separated by commas, so a comma goes after "musicians" to match the comma after "garden." The semicolon fails because the list items contain no commas of their own.
ce: A colon cannot appear in the middle of a list.
A single dash signals emphasis or an interruption; it cannot separate ordinary items in a list that already uses commas.
A semicolon would separate list items only if the items already contained commas, and here they do not.
Correct: a comma separates the second item in the list from the third, which begins with "and."

questions.p: After years of testing, the engineers finally settled on a single material for the blades of the new wind ______ carbon fibre, which is both lighter and stronger than the steel used in older designs.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The first part is a complete sentence that promises a material, and a colon introduces it. The semicolon fails because what follows is not a complete sentence.
ce: A semicolon needs a complete sentence after it, and "carbon fibre, which is…" is only a noun with a description.
Correct: a complete sentence comes before, and a colon introduces the material that it names.
"Which carbon fibre…" is not a correct clause, so the sentence becomes ungrammatical.
With no punctuation, "turbine carbon fibre" runs together and the sentence does not read correctly.

questions.p: The 1883 eruption of the Indonesian volcano ______ was so loud that it was heard more than 4,000 kilometers away, on an island in the Indian Ocean.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "The 1883 eruption of the Indonesian volcano Krakatoa" is the subject and "was" is its verb, so no punctuation is needed. A comma is the trap after a long subject, but it must not separate subject and verb.
ce: A single dash would wrongly split the subject from its verb.
A single comma would separate the subject from its verb "was."
A semicolon would cut the subject off from its verb.
Correct: the name is essential to the subject "The 1883 eruption of the Indonesian volcano Krakatoa," and no punctuation goes between the subject and its verb "was."

questions.p: Scientists have been sampling the seawater off one coast every year since 2005. The number of tiny plastic particles found in each sample ______ increased steadily since the first measurements were taken.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The subject is "The number," which is singular, so "has." "Have" is the trap because the plural "particles" comes right before the blank.
ce: Plural, and "were increased" does not fit a period that runs up to the present.
Plural verb: it agrees with "particles" or "samples," which are not the subject.
Correct: the subject is "The number" (singular), and "since" calls for the present perfect: "has increased."
Plural, and "are increased" does not fit a period that started in the past and continues to now.

questions.p: Emily Brontë's only novel, Wuthering Heights, ______ in 1847, about a year before her death. At first, many reviewers found its wild, stormy story shocking.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: A specific past date calls for the simple past: "was published." "Has been published" is the trap, but the present perfect does not go with a finished time like 1847.
ce: Present tense does not fit an event in 1847.
Correct: "in 1847" names a finished time in the past, so the simple past is needed.
The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time such as "in 1847."
The past perfect progressive is illogical for a book, which cannot be doing the publishing itself.

questions.p: After the local factory closed, a team of sociologists spent two years in the neighbourhood, ______ residents about how the closure had changed their daily routines.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The sentence already has its main verb ("spent"), so the added part needs a non-finite form: "interviewing." "They interviewed" creates a comma splice.
ce: Comma splice: "they interviewed residents…" is a complete sentence joined with only a comma.
Correct: the participle adds what the team did during those two years without starting a new main clause.
A noun or present-tense verb here does not fit the sentence and clashes with the past tense.
"And" needs to join two parallel parts, but "spent" and "interviewing" are not parallel.

questions.p: Diamond and graphite are both made entirely of carbon. ______ the two materials could hardly be more different: diamond is the hardest natural substance known, while graphite is so soft that it is used in pencils.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The first sentence stresses what the materials share, and the second stresses how different they are, so a contrast is needed: "Despite this." "Therefore" wrongly suggests that sharing carbon causes the difference.
ce: Being made of carbon does not cause them to be different, so a cause-effect transition is illogical.
Correct: being made of the same element would lead us to expect similarity, so their great difference is a contrast.
Their difference is not an example of both being made of carbon.
The second sentence does not add a similar point; it goes against what the first suggests.

questions.p: Animated films were once drawn entirely by hand, one frame at a time, and a single feature could require hundreds of thousands of drawings. ______ most animated feature films are created with computer software, which can generate the in-between frames of a movement automatically.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The text contrasts animation in the past with animation now, so the transition must show a change: "Today, however." "Similarly" fails because the two methods differ.
ce: Correct: it marks both a change in time and a contrast with the hand-drawn method.
Computer animation is not an example of hand drawing.
Hand drawing did not cause the use of computers; the sentence describes a later change.
Computer animation is not similar to drawing by hand; it replaced it.

questions.p: Older people are especially at risk during heat waves, and those who live alone may have no one nearby to notice if they become ill. ______ several cities now send volunteers to check on elderly residents who live alone whenever temperatures rise above a set level.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The first sentence explains a danger and the second gives a response to it, so a cause-effect transition fits: "Accordingly." "Nevertheless" fails because there is no contrast.
ce: Sending volunteers is not surprising given the risk; it is the expected response.
Correct: the volunteer visits are a response that follows logically from the risk described.
Nothing is being replaced; the visits are added because of the risk.
The visits are not similar to the risk; they are a response to it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hedy Lamarr was a film actress; George Antheil was a composer.
• In 1942, they patented an idea called frequency hopping.
• In frequency hopping, a radio signal switches rapidly among many frequencies in a pattern known only to the sender and the receiver.
• This makes the signal very hard for an enemy to block, or jam.
• Similar techniques are used today in some wireless technologies, such as Bluetooth.
questions.q: The student wants to explain what frequency hopping is. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Techniques similar to the one Lamarr and Antheil patented are used today in Bluetooth.
Hedy Lamarr, a film actress, and George Antheil, a composer, patented an idea together in 1942.

Frequency hopping, patented in 1942 by actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil, makes a radio signal hard to jam by switching it rapidly among many frequencies in a pattern known only to the sender and receiver.
Lamarr and Antheil's 1942 idea made radio signals very hard for an enemy to block.
questions.e: To explain frequency hopping, the sentence must describe the switching between frequencies and why that prevents jamming; only one choice does. The Bluetooth choice is accurate but shows a use, not an explanation.
ce: It shows the idea's later use but does not explain what it is.
It introduces the inventors but never explains the idea.
Correct: it explains what frequency hopping does and how, and names who patented it.
It gives the benefit but not how frequency hopping works.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Along some coasts, steady winds push surface water away from the shore.
• Cold water from the deep ocean rises to replace it. This is called upwelling.
• Deep water is rich in nutrients.
• The nutrients feed huge numbers of plankton, which in turn feed fish.
• Upwelling off the coast of Peru supports one of the world's largest fisheries.
questions.q: The student wants to explain why some coastal waters are especially rich in fish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Along some coasts, steady winds push surface water away from the shore.
Upwelling off the coast of Peru supports one of the world's largest fisheries.
Deep ocean water is cold and rich in nutrients.
Where winds push surface water away from a coast, cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the deep, feeding plankton and, in turn, large numbers of fish, as off the coast of Peru.
questions.e: Explaining why some coastal waters are rich in fish requires the whole cause-and-effect chain, and only one choice gives it. The Peru choice states the result without the explanation.
ce: It starts the process but stops before explaining the fish.
It gives the result but not why upwelling produces so many fish.
One link in the chain; it does not connect the nutrients to fish.
Correct: it gives the full chain from wind to upwelling to nutrients to plankton to fish.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sociologist Rana Fouad studied weekly markets in two towns, one in Egypt and one in Morocco.
• In both towns, market day is the busiest day of the week.
• In both towns, many residents said they visit the market as much to meet friends as to shop.
• The Egyptian market sells mainly food.
• The Moroccan market also sells livestock.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two markets. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Sociologist Rana Fouad studied weekly markets in two towns.
The Egyptian market Fouad studied sells mainly food, while the Moroccan market also sells livestock.
In both the Egyptian and the Moroccan town that Fouad studied, many residents said they visit the weekly market as much to meet friends as to shop.
The Moroccan market Fouad studied sells livestock.
questions.e: A similarity must describe something true of both markets; the social role of the market (meeting friends) is shared. The food-and-livestock choice is the trap: it compares the markets but shows a difference.
ce: It introduces the study but states no similarity.
This is a difference, not a similarity.
Correct: it states something the two markets share.
It describes only one market.

questions.p: Although the young pianist's technique was ______, critics complained that her performances lacked feeling: every note was perfectly placed, yet the music rarely moved them.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "Although" sets good technique against a lack of feeling, and "every note was perfectly placed" shows the technique was perfect: "flawless." "Limited" fails because the critics fault her feeling, not her skill.
ce: Correct: "every note was perfectly placed" describes technique without mistakes.
Opposite: perfectly placed notes are not clumsy.
Perfect placement of every note is consistent, not uneven.
Nothing suggests a narrow range of skills; the criticism is about feeling, not ability.

questions.p: Geologists once regarded the region as seismically ______, since no strong earthquake had been recorded there in written history. Studies of ancient soil layers disturbed by past earthquakes have since shown that powerful quakes struck the area every few thousand years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The earlier view rested on no strong earthquakes being recorded, so geologists thought the region was "inactive"; later studies showed otherwise. "Dangerous" describes the newer view, not the old one.
ce: Nothing suggests the region was well known for earthquakes; the opposite was believed.
Reversed: the later studies, not the earlier view, showed the danger.
The earlier view was based on a lack of earthquakes, not on their irregular timing.
Correct: with no recorded strong earthquakes, geologists thought the region had no earthquake activity.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Mr. Lacey's manner toward his new employer was perfectly ______: he bowed when she entered, answered every question promptly, and never offered an opinion unless it was asked for, so that she could find no fault in him, and no warmth either.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: He does everything correctly but without warmth, so his manner is "proper." "Affectionate" is ruled out by "no warmth either."
ce: Contradicted: she found "no warmth" in him.
Opposite: insolent means rude, but she "could find no fault in him."
Correct: bowing, prompt answers and no unasked opinions are correct, polite behaviour with no fault, though cold.
His behaviour is completely conventional, not strange.

questions.p: Supporters of the new solar water-purification unit do not claim that it will ______ the need for large treatment plants; they argue only that it can supply safe drinking water to villages too remote to be connected to such plants.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: Supporters make a modest claim ("only" remote villages), so the claim they avoid must be a bigger one: that the unit would remove the need for plants: "eliminate." "Support" fails because it is not a bold claim to back away from.
ce: Showing a need is not the kind of large claim that the modest "only" claim is set against.
The contrast with "only" requires a strong claim that supporters avoid; supporting the need for plants is not such a claim.
A purification unit cannot pay for a need, so the phrase makes no sense.
Correct: supporters do not claim the unit will remove the need for plants; they claim only a smaller role for it.

questions.p: Interviews with residents revealed that the new housing development's effect on the neighbourhood was ______: some long-time residents welcomed the new shops and cafés, while others complained that rising rents were forcing their friends to move away.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The colon gives both good and bad effects, so the overall effect was "mixed." "Uniform" is the opposite of what the different reactions show.
ce: Correct: some residents saw benefits and others saw harm, so the effect was mixed.
Contradicted: residents describe clear changes, both good and bad, so the effect was not tiny.
Opposite: residents reacted in different ways, so the effect was not the same for everyone.
Nothing in the text says the effects will end.

questions.p: Most of the deep ocean floor has never been mapped in fine detail. Satellites can estimate the shape of the sea floor by measuring tiny bumps in the ocean surface, but these maps show only features several kilometers across. Detailed maps require ships that bounce sound off the sea floor, and such surveys are slow and costly. As a result, scientists today have more detailed maps of the surface of Mars than of much of Earth's own ocean floor.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that money should be spent on ocean maps rather than on exploring Mars
To argue that satellites are useless for studying the ocean
To describe how sound was first used to measure the depth of the sea
To explain why much of Earth's ocean floor remains poorly mapped
questions.e: The text states a problem (poor maps) and explains its causes (coarse satellite maps, slow and costly ship surveys). The Mars spending choice turns a comparison into an argument the text never makes.
ce: The Mars comparison shows how poor ocean maps are; the text makes no argument about spending.
Too extreme: satellites do produce maps, only not detailed ones.
The history of sound measurement is not discussed.
Correct: the text gives the limits of satellites and the cost of ship surveys as reasons for the poor maps.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The quarrel between the two brothers had begun over a boundary stone, though neither could now say on which side of the stone the fault had lain. For eleven years they had passed each other in the lane without a word. Then, in the hard winter of that year, the elder brother's barn caught fire in the night, and it was the younger who was first to arrive with a bucket.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It describes a long-standing conflict and then presents an event that suggests the conflict may be changing.
It explains the cause of a conflict in detail and then decides which brother was to blame.
It compares the farms of two brothers and explains why one was more successful.
It describes a fire and then explains how the fire began.
questions.e: The text sets up a long silence between the brothers and then shows the younger one helping in a crisis, hinting at reconciliation. The blame choice fails because the text says no one remembers whose fault it was.
ce: Correct: eleven years of silence, then the younger brother rushes to help, a sign of change.
Neither brother can say where the fault lay, and the text assigns no blame.
No farms are compared and no success is discussed.
The cause of the fire is never given.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many architects favour office towers with walls made almost entirely of glass. Large windows, they argue, fill workspaces with natural daylight, reducing the need for electric lighting and so saving energy.

Text 2
Engineer Yasmin Qadri points out that in hot, sunny climates, all-glass walls let in so much heat from the sun that the extra cost of air-conditioning can be greater than the savings on lighting. She recommends windows shaded by deep overhangs or carved screens, which let in daylight while blocking direct sunlight.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Qadri (Text 2) most likely respond to the architects' argument in Text 1?
c: She would argue that natural daylight does not reduce the need for electric lighting.
She would agree that daylight can reduce the need for electric lighting but argue that in hot climates, all-glass walls may increase total energy use.
She would recommend building more all-glass towers in hot climates.
She would claim that air-conditioning always costs less than electric lighting.
questions.e: Qadri grants the architects' point about daylight but adds that, in hot climates, the heat cost can be bigger than the saving. The "daylight does not reduce lighting" choice ignores that she accepts the savings.
ce: Contradicted: she speaks of "savings on lighting," so she accepts that daylight helps.
Correct: she accepts lighting savings but says cooling costs can outweigh them.
Reversed: she recommends shaded windows instead.
She says the opposite can happen: cooling costs can exceed lighting savings.

questions.p: While a film is being edited, the director often places existing music, called a temp track, under scenes before the real score has been written. The temp track helps editors judge the pace and mood of each scene. Many film composers, however, dislike the practice. Directors can grow so attached to the temporary music after hearing it many times that they ask the composer to write something almost identical, leaving little room for original ideas.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Temp tracks help editors judge the pace and mood of each scene.
Although temp tracks help editors judge scenes, they can limit composers' originality when directors become attached to them.
Composers usually write temp tracks before a film is edited.
Most temp tracks are kept in the final versions of films.
questions.e: The text presents a use of temp tracks and then, after "however," its downside for composers; the main idea combines both. The pace-and-mood choice is only half of it.
ce: Too narrow: only the benefit, not the problem the text stresses.
Correct: it joins the benefit and the main problem that the text develops after "however."
Contradicted: temp tracks are existing music used before the composer's score.
Not supported: the text says directors want something similar, not that the temp music is kept.

questions.p: Sociologist Ola Bassiouny hypothesizes that residents trust their neighbours more on streets where children play outdoors, because parents watching their children outside get to know the other adults on the street.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bassiouny's hypothesis?
c: After one city closed some residential streets to traffic on weekend afternoons so that children could play there, residents' trust in their neighbours rose over the following year, but it stayed the same on similar streets that remained open to traffic.
Streets where many children live have more parked cars than streets where few children live.
Residents who have lived on a street for many years trust their neighbours more than newer residents do.
Parents say they spend more time outdoors on weekends than adults without children do.
questions.e: The hypothesis links outdoor play to trust, and the street-closure finding shows trust rising only where play increased, compared with similar streets. The length-of-residence choice offers a different explanation instead.
ce: Correct: when outdoor play increased, trust rose, while similar streets without the change saw no rise.
Parked cars have nothing to do with trust between neighbours.
This points to length of residence, not outdoor play, as a cause of trust.
It shows parents are outside more but not that this builds trust.

questions.p: In an original novel written in the style of the nineteenth century, the narrator suggests that the town's new wealth has made many of its leading citizens ashamed of their humble beginnings.
questions.q: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "The merchants who now drove to church in carriages had, most of them, walked to it barefoot as boys, though none of them cared to be reminded of the fact."
"The town's new bank was built of grey granite and was the pride of the high street."
"Every Saturday the market square was crowded with farmers from the hills."
"The old mill by the river had stood empty for many years."
questions.e: The claim joins new wealth with shame about humble origins, and only the barefoot-boys quotation shows both. The bank quotation shows wealth but nothing about the past.
ce: Correct: it shows both the new wealth (carriages) and the wish to forget their poor past.
It shows wealth but not any feeling about the past.
It describes market day, not wealth or shame.
It describes a building, not the citizens' attitude.

questions.p:
Adults who report often feeling lonely, by living situation and age (%)
Living situation | Ages 18–34 | Ages 35–64 | Ages 65 and over
Living alone | 38 | 29 | 24
Living with others | 21 | 14 | 12

A sociologist analyzing a national survey argues that living alone is linked to loneliness in every age group, but that the link is strongest among the youngest adults.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the sociologist's argument?
c: Among people living with others, those aged 18 to 34 were the most likely to feel lonely.
In every age group, a higher percentage of people living alone than of people living with others often felt lonely.
Among people aged 65 and over, 24% of those living alone often felt lonely.
Among 18- to 34-year-olds, 38% of those living alone often felt lonely, compared with 21% of those living with others, a gap of 17 points, larger than the gap for either older group.
questions.e: The argument has two parts, so the answer must show a gap and show that the youngest group's gap is the largest: 17 points vs 15 (ages 35–64) and 12 (65+). The "every age group" choice is true but covers only the first part.
ce: True, but it describes only people who live with others, so it says nothing about the effect of living alone.
True, but it supports only the first part of the argument, not that the link is strongest for the youngest.
True, but one figure for one group cannot show a link or compare age groups.
Correct: it supports both parts, showing a gap and showing that the youngest group's gap (17) is larger than the others (15 and 12).

questions.p:
Average retreat of four glaciers in one mountain range (meters per year)
Glacier | Direction the glacier faces | 1990–2005 | 2005–2020
Alda | North | 8 | 11
Brenn | South | 15 | 24
Corvo | North | 6 | 10
Dena | South | 18 | 27

In this mountain range, which lies in the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive more direct sunlight than north-facing ones. Researchers studying four glaciers there noted that the south-facing glaciers retreated faster than the north-facing glaciers in both periods.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' observation?
c: Alda retreated faster than Brenn from 1990 to 2005.
All four glaciers retreated faster in 2005–2020 than in 1990–2005.
Dena retreated faster than any other glacier in the table from 2005 to 2020.
In both periods, the south-facing glaciers retreated by 15 to 27 meters per year, whereas the north-facing glaciers retreated by only 6 to 11 meters per year.
questions.e: The observation compares south-facing and north-facing glaciers in both periods, so the answer must cover both groups and both periods. The "all four retreated faster" choice is true but compares periods instead of directions.
ce: False: Alda retreated 8 meters per year and Brenn 15.
True, but it compares time periods, not the direction the glaciers face.
True, but one glacier in one period cannot show a difference between the two groups.
Correct: every south-facing figure (15, 18, 24, 27) is higher than every north-facing figure (6, 8, 10, 11), in both periods.

questions.p: A lighthouse needs a lens that gathers the light of its lamp into a strong beam that can be seen far out at sea. A solid glass lens large and powerful enough to do this would be extremely thick and heavy. In the early nineteenth century, the French engineer Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed a lens made of rings of carefully shaped glass prisms. The rings kept the light-bending shape of a curved lens's surface but did away with most of the glass behind it. Fresnel's design most likely allowed lighthouses to ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: stop using lamps and rely on sunlight reflected by the lens.
use large, powerful lenses that were much thinner and lighter than solid lenses of the same power.
use smaller, weaker beams that could be seen only close to shore.
make their lenses thicker in order to bend light more strongly.
questions.e: The problem was weight and thickness; Fresnel's rings kept the useful surface and removed the bulk, so lighthouses could have powerful lenses that were far lighter. The "thicker lenses" choice reverses the design's purpose.
ce: Nothing in the text suggests replacing the lamp.
Correct: keeping the light-bending surface while removing most of the glass gives the same power with far less weight.
Reversed: the purpose of the lens is a strong beam seen far out at sea.
Contradicted: the design removed most of the glass, making lenses thinner.

questions.p: Economists have often assumed that people accept long daily commutes only when they are fully compensated, for example by higher pay or a larger home, so that long-distance commuters end up no worse off overall than people who live near their work. But a team of researchers found that people with longer commutes reported lower satisfaction with their lives, even after the researchers took differences in income and home size into account. These findings suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the economists' assumption about commuters has been confirmed.
people with long commutes usually earn less than people who live near their work.
the benefits that commuters gain from living farther away may not fully make up for the costs of the commute itself.
larger homes make people less satisfied with their lives.
questions.e: The economists predicted commuters would be no worse off; the study found them less satisfied even with pay and home size counted, so the compensation seems incomplete. The "confirmed" choice reverses the findings.
ce: Reversed: lower satisfaction among commuters goes against the assumption.
Not supported: the researchers took income into account; the text does not say commuters earn less.
Correct: if commuters are less satisfied even with pay and housing counted, the benefits do not fully balance the cost.
Not supported: home size was controlled for and is not blamed for lower satisfaction.

questions.p: The ensemble's spring tour took it to three cities: Tunis, where it opened a jazz festival; Beirut, where it recorded an album with local ______ and Amman, where it gave free concerts in public parks.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Each city in the list carries a description with a comma, so the items are separated by semicolons, as after "festival." The comma is the trap: it would not match the first separator.
ce: Correct: the list items contain commas, so semicolons separate them (the SAT/ACT extra rule), matching the semicolon after "festival."
A comma does not match the semicolon used after the first item and blurs where the second item ends.
No punctuation runs the second and third items together.
A colon already introduces the list; another colon cannot separate list items.

questions.p: Most of the salt in the ocean comes from rocks on land, which are slowly broken down by rain and carried to the sea by ______ some of it, however, enters the ocean through hot springs on the sea floor.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both parts are complete sentences, so a semicolon is needed; "however" is only an interrupter inside the second clause and cannot join sentences. A comma alone makes a comma splice.
ce: Correct: "some of it, however, enters…" is a complete sentence, so a semicolon is needed before it; "however" sits inside the second clause.
Comma splice: two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma, even with "however" in the second one.
Run-on: the two sentences are fused with no punctuation.
With "and," the second clause would need no "however," and the result reads as two linked additions rather than a contrast; the contrast word then clashes with the joining word.

questions.p: Jane Austen's novel Pride and ______ was first published in 1813, opens with one of the most often quoted sentences in English literature.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Which was first published in 1813" is extra information about the novel, closed by the comma after "1813," so it must also open with a comma. The dash fails because dash…comma is not a matching pair.
ce: A semicolon would cut the subject off from its verb "opens."
Without the opening comma, the extra information is not set off, and the comma after "1813" has no partner.
Correct: the comma opens the extra information "which was first published in 1813," and it closes with the comma after "1813."
A dash cannot pair with the comma that closes the extra information after "1813."

questions.p: Measurements made by satellites since the early 1990s show ______ global sea level has been rising at an increasing rate.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "That global sea level has been rising" is what the measurements show, so it follows the verb with no punctuation. Commas around "that" are a common trap: they split a verb from its object.
ce: A comma before "that" separates the verb "show" from its object.
A comma after "that" wrongly separates it from the clause it introduces.
Correct: "that global sea level has been rising…" is the object of "show," and no punctuation goes between a verb and its object.
A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "Measurements… show that" is not one.

questions.p: Neither the architects who designed the new footbridge nor the city's mayor ______ to have expected that it would become one of the most photographed sights in the city.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: In a "neither… nor" subject, the verb agrees with the nearer part: "the city's mayor" (singular), so "seems." "Seem" is the trap: it agrees with the farther subject, "architects."
ce: Plural verb; the nearer subject, the singular "mayor," needs a singular verb such as "seems."
Plural: it agrees with "architects," but the nearer subject "mayor" decides the verb.
Plural, and the progressive form is not used with "seem" here.
Correct: with "neither… nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "the city's mayor," which is singular.

questions.p: Octopuses can change both the colour and the texture of their skin in less than a second, a skill ______ them to hide from predators by blending into the rocks around them.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "A skill" is singular, so the clause describing it needs a singular verb: "that allows." Both plural choices agree with "them" or "octopuses" instead of "skill."
ce: Correct: "that allows" describes "a skill," and the singular verb agrees with "skill."
Plural verb: "skill" is singular, so it needs "allows."
Plural verb: "which" refers to the singular "skill," so it needs "allows."
"A skill it allows them to hide" is ungrammatical: "it allows" begins a new clause that cannot attach to "a skill."

questions.p: According to United Nations estimates, between 1950 and 2020 the share of the world's population living in cities ______ from under 30 percent to more than 55 percent.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The change happened within a closed past period, so the simple past "rose" is needed. "Has risen" is tempting, but it does not fit a period that ended in 2020.
ce: Future tense contradicts the past dates.
The present perfect does not go with a period that has a fixed end in the past.
Present tense does not fit a change that took place between 1950 and 2020.
Correct: "between 1950 and 2020" is a finished period in the past, so the simple past fits.

questions.p: Around 1900, electric cars were common on the streets of American cities and, for a time, sold better than cars powered by gasoline. ______ by the 1920s they had almost vanished, as cheaper gasoline cars that could travel much farther took over the market.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The first sentence describes success and the second describes decline, so a contrast is needed: "However." "Thus" wrongly makes success the cause of the decline.
ce: Early success did not cause electric cars to vanish.
"Indeed" would strengthen the first point, but the second sentence goes against it.
Correct: electric cars almost vanishing is the opposite of their early success.
Vanishing is not similar to selling well.

questions.p: Some music researchers argue that streaming and shuffle play have changed how artists release their work. When listeners rarely hear an album from beginning to end, the order of its songs, and the idea of the album as a single connected work, matter less. ______ many artists now release songs one at a time instead of planning full albums around a single theme.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: Albums matter less, so artists release single songs: a cause and its effect, "Accordingly." "Nonetheless" fails because the result is expected, not surprising.
ce: The sentence describes what artists do now, not what they did before.
Releasing single songs is not the opposite of albums mattering less; it is a result of it.
There is no surprise: single releases are what we would expect.
Correct: releasing single songs follows logically from albums mattering less.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lev Kuleshov was a Soviet filmmaker.
• Around 1920, he showed audiences the same shot of an actor's expressionless face.
• Each time, he placed the face next to a different image: a bowl of soup, a child in a coffin, and other scenes.
• Viewers said the actor looked hungry beside the soup and sad beside the coffin.
• The experiment suggested that viewers interpret a shot partly from the shots around it.
questions.q: The student wants to explain the significance of Kuleshov's experiment. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: In Kuleshov's experiment, an actor's face was shown next to a bowl of soup and a child in a coffin.
Around 1920, Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov showed audiences the same shot of an actor's expressionless face.
Kuleshov's experiment suggested that viewers interpret a shot partly from the shots around it: the same expressionless face seemed hungry beside a bowl of soup and sad beside a coffin.
Lev Kuleshov was a Soviet filmmaker who worked around 1920.
questions.e: The significance is what the experiment revealed about how viewers read shots, and the best answer states it and backs it with the hungry/sad results. The method-only choice describes the setup without the conclusion.
ce: It gives details of the setup but not its significance.
It describes the method but not what the experiment showed.
Correct: it states what the experiment showed and supports it with the results.
Background about the filmmaker only.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many people notice a pleasant, earthy smell when rain falls after a dry spell.
• In 1964, two Australian scientists, Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas, named this smell "petrichor."
• Part of the smell comes from oils that plants release during dry periods.
• Another part comes from geosmin, a chemical produced by bacteria in the soil.
• Humans can detect geosmin even in extremely small amounts.
questions.q: The student wants to explain what causes petrichor to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Petrichor, the earthy smell that often follows rain after a dry spell, comes partly from oils released by plants and partly from geosmin, a chemical produced by bacteria in the soil.
In 1964, two Australian scientists named the smell of rain "petrichor."
Humans can detect geosmin, a chemical made by soil bacteria, even in extremely small amounts.
Part of the smell of rain comes from oils that plants release during dry periods.
questions.e: An audience unfamiliar with petrichor needs a definition plus the causes; only one choice gives both causes and explains the term. The 1964 choice gives the name's origin but no cause.
ce: Correct: it defines the term for a new audience and explains both causes of the smell.
It gives the name's history but not what causes the smell.
It explains why we notice geosmin but not what petrichor is.
Only one of the two causes, and the term is not introduced.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A superblock is a group of nine city blocks, three by three.
• Through-traffic is kept to the streets around the edge of the superblock.
• The inner streets are opened to people walking, children playing, and outdoor seating.
• Barcelona, Spain, began creating superblocks in 2016.
• Residents of some Barcelona superblocks reported less noise on the inner streets.
questions.q: The student wants to describe superblocks to an audience unfamiliar with them, using Barcelona as an example. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Barcelona, Spain, began creating superblocks in 2016.

In a superblock, such as those Barcelona began creating in 2016, through-traffic is kept to the streets around a group of nine city blocks, freeing the inner streets for walking, play, and outdoor seating.
Residents of some Barcelona superblocks reported less noise on the inner streets.
A superblock is a group of nine city blocks, three by three.
questions.e: The goal asks for a description of superblocks using Barcelona as an example; only one choice explains how the traffic and inner streets work and names Barcelona. The noise choice gives an effect, not a description.
ce: It names the example but does not describe what a superblock is.
Correct: it explains what a superblock is and uses Barcelona as the example, as the goal requires.
It gives a result but does not explain what a superblock is.
A partial definition with no mention of traffic or of Barcelona.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Read every explanation**, including those for questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason, not by luck. Each choice has its own short reason.

**List your weak skills.** Use your score by skill and write down every skill where you lost two or more questions, plus the trap that caught you (reversed, too extreme, half-right, off-topic, nearest-noun, comma splice…). The "Study these again" links take you straight to the lessons.

**Go back to the matching lessons:** Words in Context and High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs; Semicolons; Colons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement; Verb Tense and Aspect; Verb Finiteness; Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).

**Redo every question you missed** after the lesson and its practice page, without looking at the explanation, and say aloud why each wrong choice is wrong. Then go back to the practice pages of your weakest lessons and then retake the test you found hardest under the same timed conditions.
**Check your timing.** If you did not finish a module, study Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question before your next full test.
